narrative.overview:
The product is a memo, and the interface is the desk it sits on. Everything the reader sees is set like a document someone took trouble over: warm paper rather than white, a serif voice for the sentences a person would say aloud, a sans for the working parts, and a monospace whisper for the things a machine wrote down, stamps, rule ids, section eyebrows. The page is calm and unhurried. One idea per card, hairlines instead of boxes, and nothing that moves unless a run has just landed.

Colour is meaning, never decoration. Six status hues exist only to say pass, conditional, fail, uncertain, not applicable or info, and the same hue that marks a status word also tints the card that carries the answer. One deep blue belongs to the things you can touch: the Run button, the step you are on, links, focus, the caret. Three regions tell the reader where they are: the cool pane where facts are entered, the paper where the memo is read, and the sand band where it leaves for a file or for Revit. The massing drawings keep their own three tones, blue for proposed, grey for outright, amber for the staff benchmark, because those are the memo's own figures.

Two things it is not, confirmed: not a dashboard (no gauges, KPI tiles, charts for their own sake, no icon-and-heading cards as page structure) and not a startup landing page (no gradients, glass, hero numbers, floating shadows or marketing voice).
keyCharacteristics: Three voices: serif for human sentences, sans for the interface and body, mono for stamps and labels.
Paper and ink first; dark mode is composed from warm near-black, not inverted.
Status is always a word; its colour only accompanies it.
One accent, deep blue, for interactive elements only.
Flat surfaces separated by hairlines; the only shadow belongs to the walkthrough card.
Cards wear a faint wash in the hue of the answer they give.

rules.name: The Status-Only Rule
rules.body: A status hue appears only where a status word is printed or where a card carries that status. It never colours a button, a heading, a chart or a decoration.

rules.name: The One Hand Rule
rules.body: Deep blue marks what the reader can act on and nothing else. If an element is blue, it can be clicked or typed into.

rules.name: The Written Word Rule
rules.body: Colour accompanies a status; it never carries it alone. Every pill, verdict and chip prints its word.

rules.name: The Lead Sentence Rule
rules.body: In any finding, the first sentence is Ink and the continuation is grey. Hierarchy inside a paragraph comes from colour, not weight.

rules.name: The Eyebrow Rule
rules.body: Section eyebrows are mono, 11px, uppercase, tracked 0.08em, and sit above a serif heading. They are the brief's own device and stay.

rules.name: The Hairline Rule
rules.body: Depth is drawn, not cast. A card is a hairline and a change of tone; nothing at rest has a shadow.

dos: Do print every status as a word and let its hue accompany it; a pill, a verdict word, a card wash.
Do keep Deep Blue for things the reader can act on, and give the active step, links and focus that blue.
Do set the memo's sentences in Fraunces at 40 / 28 / 20px and keep body Inter at 16px with 1.5 line height.
Do separate surfaces with 1px hairlines and tone; keep cards at 8px radius and 22px padding.
Do compose dark mode from Night Paper and Night Card with the lifted status inks; check every pair stays above 4.5:1.
Do keep the figures' three tones, blue proposed, grey outright, amber benchmark, exactly as drawn.
donts: Don't build a dashboard: no gauges, KPI tiles, sparklines, or icon-plus-heading cards as structure.
Don't reach for a landing page's kit: no gradients, glass, hero numbers, floating shadows, marketing voice.
Don't put a status hue on a button, a heading, a chart or a background that carries no status.
Don't add a second accent, a coloured side border, or a shadow on anything that is not the walkthrough card.
Don't animate anything but the 150ms fade when a run lands and the walkthrough spotlight's fade; honour reduced motion.
Don't use "N/A", icons in place of words, or a checkbox where "not sure" is a legitimate answer.
